<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document">Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures<span class="ltx_pubnotes"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_thanks"><span class="ltx_note_name">Thanks: </span><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Songrun He is at Washington University in St. Louis (<a href="mailto:h.songrun@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">h.songrun@wustl.edu</a>). Asaf Manela is at Washington University in St. Louis and Reichman University (<a href="mailto:amanela@wustl.edu" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">amanela@wustl.edu</a>). Omri Ross is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:omri@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">omri@di.ku.dk</a>), and Chief Blockchain Scientist at the eToro Group. Victor von Wachter is at University of Copenhagen (<a href="mailto:victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">victor.vonwachter@di.ku.dk</a>).
We are grateful to seminar participants at a16z Crypto and at Reichman University for helpful comments.</span></span></span></span></h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Songrun He
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Asaf Manela
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Omri Ross
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Victor von Wachter
</span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">First draft December 2022. This draft April 2023.</div>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Abstract</span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures—swap contracts that never expire—are the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, with more than $100 billion traded daily.
Perpetuals provide investors with leveraged exposure to cryptocurrencies, which does not require rollover or direct cryptocurrency holding.
To keep the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices small, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a funding rate proportional to this gap. The funding rate incentivizes trades that tend to narrow the futures-spot gap.
But unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any time, and familiar no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not available, as the contracts have no expiry date to enforce arbitrage.
Here, using a weaker notion of random-maturity arbitrage, we derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and no-arbitrage bounds for markets with trading costs.
These no-arbitrage prices provide a valuable benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values.
Empirically, we find that deviations of crypto perpetual futures from no-arbitrage prices are considerably larger than those documented in traditional currency markets. These deviations comove across cryptocurrencies and diminish over time as crypto markets develop and become more efficient. A simple trading strategy generates large Sharpe ratios even for investors paying the highest trading costs on Binance, which is currently the largest crypto exchange by volume.
<span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JEL Classification</span>: G11, G12, G13 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Keywords</span>: Perpetual futures, crypto, random-maturity arbitrage, funding rate</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures are, by far, the most popular derivative traded in cryptocurrency markets, generating a daily volume of more than $100 billion.
Prior to the recent collapse of FTX, perpetual futures were among the most actively-traded products on the exchange, with the now-bankrupt hedge fund Alameda Research taking the other side of many such leveraged trades. Despite their central role in crypto markets, there is relatively little work studying these derivatives. In this paper we ask: what are the theoretical fundamental values of perpetual futures, and how large are deviations from these fundamentals empirically?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetuals are a derivative that allows investors to speculate on or hedge against cryptocurrency price fluctuations using high leverage, without taking delivery of cryptocurrencies and without needing to roll them overs. In essence, perpetuals are agreements between long and short counterparties. The party on the short side is required to pay the long side a sum based on the increase in the futures price between when they enter and exit the contract. Meanwhile, the long side pays the short side an ongoing cash flow called the “funding rate”. Different from traditional futures, perpetual futures do not have an expiration date. Both parties can enter or exit the contract at any time, and profits or losses are continually calculated and allocated to each side’s margin account. This setup improves the liquidity of the contract because there is no staggering of contracts with different maturities traded on the exchange and only a single perpetual futures contract per underlying is traded. Furthermore, this instrument does not require market participants to deal with rolling over of their futures positions and is traded 24/7.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike fixed-maturity futures, perpetuals are not guaranteed to converge to the spot price of their underlying asset at any time, and familiar no-arbitrage prices for perpetuals are not available.
To keep the gap between perpetual futures and spot prices small, long position holders periodically pay short position holders a funding rate proportional to this gap to incentivize trades that tend to narrow it.
For example, when the futures price exceeds the spot price, arbitrageurs who borrow cash to long the spot and simultaneously short the futures would collect the funding rate. Their trades would tend to increase the spot price and decrease the futures price.
A narrow gap means that perpetual futures provide effective exposure to variation in the spot price of the underlying asset to hedging and speculating investors. In practice, the funding rate is typically paid every eight hours and approximately equals the average futures-spot spread over the preceding eight hours.
Note that the strategy just sketched, commonly referred to as “funding rate arbitrage,” is not risk-free even if one ignores margin requirements and trading costs, simply because there is no predetermined maturity date when the trade would be unwound at a profit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures in frictionless markets and derive no-arbitrage bounds in markets with trading costs.
The theoretical perpetual futures price is proportional to the spot price of the underlying, with a constant of proportionality that increases in the ratio of the interest rate to the funding rate. The interest rate captures the cost of borrowing cash to finance holding the underlying, while the funding rate captures the benefit of shorting the futures.
Thus, intuitively, the future-spot spread is larger when the cash borrowing interest rate is large relative to the funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our derivation relies on a weaker notion of arbitrage that we call <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em>. As its name suggests, unlike traditional riskless arbitrage, we allow the strategy’s time-to-maturity to be random. At first glance, one might object that such prices are not truly based on riskless arbitrage. Note, however, that riskless no-arbitrage pricing is usually just a useful fiction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedersen, 2019</a>)</cite>. For example, in real-world futures markets, arbitrageurs must maintain a margin account during the entire period in which the arbitrage trade is open. Temporary worsening of apparent arbitrage opportunities can lead to liquidations and losses. As the saying goes, an arbitrageur must remain liquid longer than the market stays irrational. Thus, even arbitrage opportunities that appear to be riskless in theory, may be risky in practice.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">These no-arbitrage prices provide a useful benchmark for perpetual futures and simultaneously prescribe a strategy to exploit divergence from these fundamental values.
Motivated by the theoretical understanding, we study the empirical deviations of the perpetual futures price from the spot.
The mean absolute futures-spot spread is about 60% to 100% per year across different cryptocurrencies, which is considerably larger than the deviations documented in traditional currency markets by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.
We find strong comovement of the futures-spot gap across different cryptocurrencies. This comovement can be due to commonality in funding and market liquidity faced by arbitrageurs who operate in multiple cryptocurrencies. Common sentiment could also drive the difference in futures demand relative to the spot. Overall, the magnitude of the deviation is comparable to our theoretic no-arbitrage bound calibrated to actual trading fees.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The spread narrows considerably in 2022, suggesting a decrease in arbitrage frictions in the market and an increase in competition among arbitrageurs. The narrowing gap provides an additional perspective on the downfall of Alameda Research and Three Arrows Capital. According to news reports and interviews, both hedge funds seem to have pivoted from such arbitrage activity around late 2021 to early 2022 and started taking more directional bets on cryptocurrencies, with both direct unhedged crypto holdings and investments in crypto startups. The large declines in crypto prices in 2022 subsequently exhausted their capital and led to their bankruptcies.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          See, for example, Forbes, November 19, 2022, on <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeffkauflin/2022/11/19/how-did-sam-bankman-frieds-alameda-research-lose-so-much-money" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">How Did Sam Bankman-Fried’s Alameda Research Lose So Much Money?</a>, Odd Lots, November 17, 2022, on <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-17/odd-lots-podcast-understanding-sam-bankman-fried-s-ftx-crypto-collapse" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Understanding the Collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s Crypto Empire</a>, and Hugh Hendry’s interview on December 3 2022 of Kyle Davies on the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TzGdkB0xbCE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Collapse of Three Arrows Capital</a>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the economics of the futures-spot spread, we consider a trading strategy motivated by the random-maturity arbitrage theory. Whenever the futures-spot spread exceeds the theoretical bound under certain trading cost tiers, we open the trading position and close it when the futures-spot spread returns to its theoretical relationship under no trading costs. We find that empirically, the random maturity arbitrage strategy generates a sizable Sharpe ratio even under high trading costs. For example, for Bitcoin perpetual futures, the strategy can generate a Sharpe ratio of 1.92 under high trading costs typical of retail investors, and up to 3.94 for highly-active market makers who pay no such fees. The performance is even better for ETH and other cryptocurrencies. The strategies deliver significant alphas relative to the 3-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu, Tsyvinski, and Wu (2022)</a></cite> and the 5-factor model of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Karolyi, Tang, and
Zhao (2022b)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">What explains these large no-arbitrage deviations?
One natural explanation is that liquidity in crypto markets is insufficient for arbitrageurs to eliminate such violations. Our finding that the spreads decline over time is consistent with liquidity improving as these markets develop, and leaves open the possibility that they will narrow going forward.
We also find, however, that past return momentum significantly explains the futures-spot gap with a time-series regression <math id="S1.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> of more than <math id="S1.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math>. When past returns are high, futures tend to be traded at a higher price relative to the spot. This indicates positive feedback or momentum trading behavior in the perpetual futures market. This correlation may linger even as crypto markets become more efficient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The existing literature on perpetual futures mainly focuses on descriptive evidence. See e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alexander, Choi, Park, and
Sohn (2020)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Franz and Schmeling (2021)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">De Blasis and Webb (2022)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ferko, Moin, Onur, and Penick (2022)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Streltsov and Ruan (2022)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angeris, Chitra, Evans, and
Lorig (2022)</a></cite> provide a theoretical no-arbitrage analysis of the perpetual but they make over-simplifying assumptions by assuming the payoff from the perpetual is a fixed function of the underlying spot price. Compared to the existing literature, we illustrate the fundamental mechanism behind the perpetual design and derive theoretical no-arbitrage prices and bounds for this instrument.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Also related is recent literature on fixed maturity futures in the crypto space. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmeling, Schrimpf, and
Karamfil (2022)</a></cite> provides a comprehensive analysis of the carry of crypto futures, with the carry defined following the general definition of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen, and
Vrugt (2018)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmeling, Schrimpf, and
Karamfil (2022)</a></cite> document a volatile convenience yield in the crypto space driven by high leverage from trend-chasing small investors and the relative scarcity of arbitrage capital. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, He, and Tang (2022a)</a></cite> provide a novel link of the volatile convenience yield to the staking, service flow, and transaction convenience of the underlying tokens. They show that the large deviation from uncovered interest rate parity can be reconciled with transaction convenience. Our paper focuses on perpetual futures rather than fixed maturity futures and extends fixed-maturity to random-maturity no-arbitrage pricing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">More broadly, our paper contributes to the understanding of the frictions and arbitrage in cryptocurrency markets. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Makarov and Schoar (2020)</a></cite> study price deviations across exchanges. They find large gaps across countries, highlighting the important role played by capital controls and slow-moving arbitrage capital as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duffie (2010)</a></cite>. Our analysis focuses on the price wedge between the spot and the futures market. We find that even within an exchange, futures prices deviate from their theoretical arbitrage-free values. These results indicate there are significant limits to arbitrage as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gromb and Vayanos (2018)</a></cite> for cryptocurrencies in the early years.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section <a href="#S2" title="2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides the institutional details and history of perpetual futures. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the no-arbitrage analysis of the perpetual futures market and derives the theoretical price of perpetual futures. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> demonstrates the empirical futures-spot deviation and presents the simple theory-motivated trading strategy that can exploit the arbitrage opportunity. Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides some explanation for the deviation between futures and the spot. Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusion ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> concludes.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>An Introduction to Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The idea of perpetual futures was first introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shiller (1993)</a></cite>. The goal was to set up a perpetual claim on the cash flows of an illiquid asset. For example, the cash flow can be house rents and the underlying illiquid asset can be the real estate market. The purpose of the perpetual futures is to enable price discovery for the underlying with an illiquid or hard-to-measure price. Perpetual futures have no expiration date but cash is exchanged between the long and the short side: after buying the perpetual futures, the long side is entitled to receive the flow cash flow from the short side and they settle the price difference when exiting the position.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v3/figures/exchange_volume_v2.png" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/181;" width="476" height="181" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Total trading volumes of perpetual futures across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure displays the 7-day moving average daily traded volume for perpetual futures across all exchanges in blue. The median daily volume is $17.8 bn. (2020), $132.0 bn. (2021) and $101.9 bn. (2022). This translates to a yearly volume of $8,551 bn. (2020), $51,989 bn. (2021) and $39,306 bn. (2022) respectively. Additionally, the grey line depicts the ratio between the traded volume in perpetuals and spot markets. In 2022 the Perpetual markets are consistently trading between 2x or 3.5x the spot volume. The data is obtained from CoinGecko, a crypto data specialist. We exclude exchanges that are known for misrepresenting data (e.g. forms of wash trading).</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures in crypto markets similarly have no expiration date and cash is exchanged between the long and the short side, but their purpose is different from Shiller’s original idea. First, unlike, e.g. real estate market, crypto has no inherent dividend or cash flow. Second, the price discovery argument of Shiller is most applicable to settings where spot prices are difficult to measure. Crypto spot prices, however, can be measured from active trading on different exchanges, and decentralized exchanges such as Bancor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hertzog et al., 2017</a>)</cite> or Uniswap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adams et al., 2021</a>)</cite> can offer price discovery for assets with minimal liquidity. The major role perpetual futures play in the crypto space is to offer an effective leveraged trading vehicle to hedge or speculate the underlying spot price movement, which makes the market more complete. It also serves as an effective tax payment optimization tool for investors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Crypto perpetual futures were first introduced by BitMEX in 2016, which gained great popularity in the crypto space since its inception. It initially served as an effective hedging tool for crypto miners. It was later adopted by crypto speculators interested in leveraged exposure. Nowadays, based on data from CoinGecko, the median total daily trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges is 101.9 billion in the year 2022 which is about <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> the total spot trading volume across these exchanges. Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the 7-day moving average of the total trading volume of perpetual futures across all exchanges. We see a significant rise in trading of perpetual futures around January 2021 and the total volume stabilizes at a level above $100 billion per day following the rise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong, Li, Tang, and
Yang (2022c)</a></cite> document significant wash trading behavior among crypto exchanges because of competition, the ranking mechanism, and lack of regulation. They estimate that over 70% of crypto trading volume is not real. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amiram, Lyandres, and
Rabetti (2020)</a></cite> confirm this conclusion using new data and an extended methodology. Therefore, in calculating trading volume, we exclude exchanges that are known to misrepresent data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v3/figures/exchanges_fr_bitcoin.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/186;" width="476" height="186" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Bitcoin annualized funding rate across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S2.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The figure presents the 7-day moving average annualized funding rate for Bitcoin (BTC) across exchanges. The data is obtained from glassnode, an analytics platform. The data covers two major market turbulences: the COVID stock market crash from February to April 2020, and the FTX insolvency in November 2022. The FTX collapse led to significant negative funding rates on all solvent exchanges, thus the perpetual future prices were lower than the spot prices on the solvent exchanges. Vice versa on the insolvent FTX. The funding rates become more volatile after the event, indicating increased uncertainty for the market participants.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A key feature of crypto perpetual futures is the funding rate, which is the cash exchanged between the long and short counterparties. Its goal is to keep the futures price close to the underlying spot so that the futures can be an effective hedging tool for spot price movement. The funding rate is typically paid every 8 hours. Its value is approximately a weighted average of the prior 8 hours’ price gap of the futures and the spot. If the futures price is above the spot, the funding rate will be positive, meaning the long side of the futures needs to pay the short side. This incentivizes traders to short the futures, and in doing so, to move its price back in line with the spot. On the other hand, when the futures price is below the spot, the funding rate turns negative, which means the short side needs to pay the long side. Therefore, the funding rate is the key mechanism keeping the futures price close to the spot price.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> provides a detailed explanation of how the funding rate is calculated.</span></span></span> Note that perpetual futures cannot be replicated by rolling over 8-hour maturity futures. For the latter, every 8 hours, the price is guaranteed to converge to the underlying spot, while for the perpetual futures this is not the case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 An Introduction to Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the annualized 7-day moving average of Bitcoin perpetual funding rates across leading exchanges from January 2020 to December 2022.
The funding rate is positive when the futures-to-spot spread is positive, and negative otherwise. Funding rates tend to be similar across exchanges due to cross-exchange arbitrage activity, but can diverge during extreme liquidity episodes. During March 2020, as Covid-19 started to spread and liquidity evaporated, funding rates turned substantially negative in most exchanges. Funding rates turned highly positive during the crypto bull run of early 2021. The last episode highlighted is the collapse of FTX, which was the 4th largest crypto exchange at the time. The figure shows that Bitcoin futures prices were substantially higher than spot prices at FTX, but the opposite was true on other exchanges. This pattern is consistent with FTX investors liquidating their short futures positions quickly, either voluntarily to reduce their exposure to the failing exchange, or involuntarily as the exchange liquidated their underfunded positions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next derive no-arbitrage prices for perpetual futures prices relative to spot prices. Unlike traditional futures, perpetual futures have no expiration date. To analyze arbitrage in this market, we extend the traditional notion of risk-free arbitrage where arbitrageurs have a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain time in the future. We first describe the payoff structure of perpetual futures. We then introduce a generalized notion of an arbitrage opportunity with a certain positive payoff but at an uncertain future time.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A perpetual future <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> written on <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> is an agreement between the long and the short side. There is <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> cost to enter the agreement. After entering, both the long side and the short side can terminate the contract at any time <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. Before termination, for each unit of perpetual future, the long must pay the short an <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{s}-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{s}-</annotation></semantics></math>adapted cash-flow <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds,\,s\in(0,t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa(F_{s}-S_{s})ds,\,s\in(0,t)</annotation></semantics></math>, referred to as the funding value. <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> is a scaling parameter determining the magnitude of the funding rate relative to the price gap. At termination, the short needs to pay the long <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}-F_{0}\," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}-F_{0}\,</annotation></semantics></math> for each unit shorted.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This definition is an approximation of real-world perpetual futures. In most exchanges, the funding value for perpetual futures is paid every <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> hours and approximately equals the difference between the futures price and the spot. If we measure time units in years, this setup would correspond to <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=1095" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1095</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=1095</annotation></semantics></math>. Consider the case where the gap is constant <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}-S_{t}=G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}-S_{t}=G</annotation></semantics></math> over the 8-hour interval. The total funding rate payment over the 8 hours would be <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\kappa G}{3\times 365}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>365</mn></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\kappa G}{3\times 365}</annotation></semantics></math>, which equals the price gap <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> in the empirical setting. Therefore, we have <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=1095" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1095</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=1095</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The traditional notions of arbitrage typically consider a guaranteed positive payoff at a certain future date.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A (riskless) arbitrage opportunity is defined with respect to payoff <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> at a certain future time <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and its price <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. If the following conditions are satisfied: (1) <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, (2) <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> with some positive probability, and (3) its price satisfies <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)\leq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then this payoff is an arbitrage opportunity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cochrane, 2009</a>)</cite>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">There is no expiration date in the perpetual futures market. Therefore, a generalized notion of arbitrage is required. Suppose the risk-free rate is constant. We define <em id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random-maturity arbitrage</em> opportunities as zero-cost strategies with a guaranteed positive payoff at an uncertain future time. Stated formally:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A random-maturity arbitrage opportunity is defined with respect to a random payoff <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> at a future random time <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}\in(0,\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}\in(0,\infty)</annotation></semantics></math>, and its price <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math>. If the following conditions are satisfied: (1) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> almost surely, (2) <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> with some positive probability, and (3) its price satisfies <math id="Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)\leq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)\leq 0</annotation></semantics></math>, then this payoff is a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Definition <a href="#Thmtheorem3" title="Definition 3. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> generalizes traditional arbitrage in the sense that there is a guaranteed positive payoff but at an uncertain future time. The following corollary specializes this definition for perpetual futures:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 1</span></span><span id="Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">In the perpetual futures market, if a strategy (1) has <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> cost at time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>, and (2) for any price path of the futures and the spot, <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>, there exists an unwinding time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> such that its discounted payoff at time <math id="Thmcorollary1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=\tilde{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=\tilde{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> is positive, then this strategy is a random-maturity arbitrage.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We next show that when there is no random-maturity arbitrage, the gap between futures and spot prices is bounded by a constant. We make the two following assumptions:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 1</span></span><span id="Thmassumption1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The gap between the perpetual futures and the spot satisfies the following condition:
<math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}|F_{t}(\omega)-S_{t}(\omega)|&lt;\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim inf</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ω</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}|F_{t}(\omega)-S_{t}(\omega)|&lt;\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmassumption1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall\,\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">∀</mo><mi>ω</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall\,\omega</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="Thmassumption2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmassumption2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption 2</span></span><span id="Thmassumption2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmassumption2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmassumption2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmassumption2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The risk-free rate <math id="Thmassumption2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> for arbitrageurs is constant.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is a no-bubble condition. <math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\liminf" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>lim inf</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\liminf</annotation></semantics></math> represents the greatest lower bound as <math id="S3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. In other words, we can always find <math id="S3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> that lie within a finite bound as <math id="S3.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. This condition
allows for the gap between <math id="S3.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to explode in the limit as long as it shrinks at some subsequent time. Assumption <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> guarantees that there is no roll-over risk for the arbitrageurs. With these two assumptions, we can state the conclusion as follows.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 1</span></span><span id="Thmproposition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage bound)<span id="Thmproposition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under Assumptions <a href="#Thmassumption1" title="Assumption 1. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#Thmassumption2" title="Assumption 2. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, when there is a constant trading cost <math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> when terminating the position, arbitrageurs will trade the perpetual futures until it lies within a bound of the spot:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C\leq F_{t}\leq S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C\leq F_{t}\leq S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">To prove this proposition, we consider the following two scenarios in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. (1) <math id="S3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})+C</annotation></semantics></math>; (2) <math id="S3.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})-C</annotation></semantics></math>. We show in the first case, the arbitrageurs want to long the spot and short the futures because this is a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity and vice versa for the second case.</span></p>
</div>

</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Discounted payoffs to arbitrage strategies in perpetual futures and spot markets</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the costs and benefits of two arbitrage trading strategies: (1) when <math id="S3.T1.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C</annotation></semantics></math>, long the spot and short the futures; (2) when <math id="S3.T1.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C</annotation></semantics></math>, long the futures and short the spot. In the last row, the payoff from exiting the position is the discounted payoff from future and spot price changes, proceeds from the cash market, and the funding rate.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 1:<span id="S3.p9.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> If <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the strategy of longing the spot and shorting the futures. We want to show that for any price path of the perpetual futures and the spot, there exists a future unwinding time <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy’s payoff is positive, that is, this is a random-maturity arbitrage. Suppose to the contrary that there exists a price path <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.p9.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall t</annotation></semantics></math>, the discounted payoff from the strategy is negative, or equivalently that:</span></span></p>
</div>

lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underbrace{e^{-rt}F_{0}-S_{0}}_{\text{traditional spread}}+\underbrace{\kappa\int_{0}^{t}(F_{s}-S_{s})e^{-rs}ds}_{\text{funding
