<div id="S3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text">Denote <math id="S3.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\equiv u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>≡</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\equiv u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the inequality changes into:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}\geq e^{-rt}(F_{0}-C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}\geq e^{-rt}(F_{0}-C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p11.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}(F_{0}-C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\underline{u}_{s}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}(F_{0}-C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\underline{u}_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.p11.2.1" class="ltx_text"> provides a lower bound for all processes <math id="S3.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying the above inequality. Solving this integral equation, we have:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\underline{u}_{t}=\frac{F_{0}re^{-rt}}{\kappa+r}+\left(\frac{F_{0}-C}{1+\frac{r}{\kappa}}-S_{0}\right)e^{\kappa t}\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\underline{u}_{t}=\frac{F_{0}re^{-rt}}{\kappa+r}+\left(\frac{F_{0}-C}{1+\frac{r}{\kappa}}-S_{0}\right)e^{\kappa t}\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="S3.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}=\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. This contradicts Assumption 1, because it implies: <math id="S3.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}\rightarrow\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim inf</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><munder accentunder="true"><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></munder><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}(F_{t}-S_{t})e^{-rt}\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\underline{u}_{t}\rightarrow\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, when <math id="S3.p12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&gt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)+C</annotation></semantics></math>, longing the spot and shorting the futures would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p13.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scenario 2:<span id="S3.p13.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Next, if <math id="S3.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C</annotation></semantics></math>, consider the strategy of longing the futures and shorting the spot. Similarly, we want to show for this strategy, for any price path of the perpetual futures and the spot, there always exists a future time <math id="S3.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> such that the strategy payoff is positive, i.e. this is a random-maturity arbitrage. Suppose not, then there exists price path <math id="S3.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{F_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p13.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{S_{t}\}_{t=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.p13.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\forall t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\forall t</annotation></semantics></math>, the discounted payoff is negative:</span></span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}\leq e^{-rt}(F_{0}+C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}\leq e^{-rt}(F_{0}+C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}u_{s}ds\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p13.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.p13.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}(F_{0}+C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\bar{u}_{s}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{u}_{t}=e^{-rt}(F_{0}+C)-S_{0}+\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\bar{u}_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.p13.2.1" class="ltx_text"> provides an upper bound for all processes <math id="S3.p13.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> satisfying the above inequality. This is the same integral equation as we see in the first case. We have:</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{u}_{t}=\frac{F_{0}re^{-rt}}{\kappa+r}+\left(\frac{F_{0}+C}{1+\frac{r}{\kappa}}-S_{0}\right)e^{\kappa t}\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfrac><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{u}_{t}=\frac{F_{0}re^{-rt}}{\kappa+r}+\left(\frac{F_{0}+C}{1+\frac{r}{\kappa}}-S_{0}\right)e^{\kappa t}\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p13.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.3.1" class="ltx_text">When <math id="S3.p13.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p13.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{u}_{t}=-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{u}_{t}=-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. This contradicts Assumption 1, because <math id="S3.p13.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}(S_{t}-F_{t})e^{-rt}\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(-\bar{u}_{t})\rightarrow\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>lim inf</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}(S_{t}-F_{t})e^{-rt}\geq\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}(-\bar{u}_{t})\rightarrow\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, when <math id="S3.p13.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}&lt;S_{0}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)-C</annotation></semantics></math>, longing futures and shorting the spot would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">No arbitrage prices are usually derived assuming away trading costs. For completeness, the following result considers this special case and provides the fundamental value of perpetual futures.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2</span></span><span id="Thmproposition2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(No-arbitrage price)<span id="Thmproposition2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">When there is no trading cost (<math id="Thmproposition2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=0</annotation></semantics></math>), arbitrageurs will trade perpetual futures toward:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{t}=S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{t}=S_{t}\left(1+\frac{r}{\kappa}\right)\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.3" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="S3.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text">The proof follows that of Proposition <math id="S3.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> by setting <math id="S3.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C=0</annotation></semantics></math>.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p16.1" class="ltx_p">To gain intuition for this result consider the first three terms of Equation (<a href="#S3.E2" title="In Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). The first is the traditional spread familiar from fixed-maturity futures pricing. Equating it to zero generates the usual no-arbitrage price for futures that pay no dividends and without carrying or storage costs. The second term is the present value of cumulated funding payments from initiation to unwinding. The first two terms are the gains to the arbitrageur in this scenario. The third term on the right hand side of the inequality is the present value of the futures-to-spot spread at the random unwinding time and is the source of tension here. For fixed-maturity futures this gap is guaranteed to be zero at expiration, but an arbitrageur in perpetual futures faces the risk that when they wish to unwind the trade the spread explodes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p17.1" class="ltx_p">Our key insight is that a positive and even modestly large spread can still leave the arbitrageur with a positive payoff because funding payments also increase with the spread. As long as the spread does not diverge to infinity, there will be some future unwinding time <math id="S3.p17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> when the accumulated funding rate payments overcome any finite potential losses at unwinding. Arbitrage is absent when the accumulated benefits due to the funding rate <math id="S3.p17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> exactly balance against the accumulated costs due to the borrowing interest rate <math id="S3.p17.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>. The no-arbitrage price (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In Proposition 2 (No-arbitrage price). ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) captures this intuition and says that the futures-spot gap increases with the ratio <math id="S3.p17.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r/\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>κ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r/\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p18.1" class="ltx_p">Note that if we relax the assumption that the short rate is constant for arbitrageurs, this may introduce some additional risk to the payoff: (1) the arbitrageur will face some risk in rolling over her borrowing in the cash market; (2) she faces some risk in reinvesting the funding payment she receives. To map into the payoff in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, this corresponds to the cash market payoff of: <math id="S3.p18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-S_{0}e^{\int_{0}^{t}r_{s}ds}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-S_{0}e^{\int_{0}^{t}r_{s}ds}</annotation></semantics></math> at time <math id="S3.p18.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> and the funding payment of <math id="S3.p18.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\int_{0}^{t}(F_{s}-S_{s})e^{\int_{s}^{t}r_{u}du}ds" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><msubsup><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em" stretchy="true">∫</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msubsup></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\int_{0}^{t}(F_{s}-S_{s})e^{\int_{s}^{t}r_{u}du}ds</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.p18.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{r_{s}\}_{s=0}^{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{r_{s}\}_{s=0}^{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math> is a stochastic process. Empirically, however, the volatility in the short rate is considerably smaller than the volatility in the gap between futures and spot prices. Moreover, the changes in the short rate have opposite effects on payment from the cash market and the funding payment. Therefore, we abstract from short rate randomness here, but note it is an interesting avenue for future work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p19" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p19.1" class="ltx_p">In the presence of trading costs, when the deviation of perpetual futures price from <math id="S3.p19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{k})</annotation></semantics></math>, is larger than the round-trip trading costs <math id="S3.p19.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, arbitrageurs would have a strong incentive to trade perpetual futures toward the price <math id="S3.p19.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>r</mi><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{0}(1+\frac{r}{\kappa})</annotation></semantics></math>. This proposition also prescribes a trading strategy to exploit the futures-spot divergence in markets with different levels of trading costs.
In the next part, we provide an empirical analysis of the futures-spot deviation and present arbitrage trading strategies motivated by our theory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Data and Empirical Analysis</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct an empirical analysis of perpetual futures arbitrage strategies. We first describe the data. We then measure the deviations of the crypto futures-spot spread from the no-arbitrage benchmark. Finally, we implement a trading strategy that exploits deviations from random-maturity no-arbitrage bounds and quantify the gains from this strategy net of trading costs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We focus on the five largest cryptocurrencies excluding the stablecoins: Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), BNB (BNB), Dogecoin (DOGE), and Cardano (ADA) with a total market cap of $529 billion, which account for 64.15% of the total market share of the Crypto market by November 2022.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each token, we obtain perpetual futures and spot prices at a 1-hour frequency from Binance. Binance is by far the leading exchange in the crypto realm. Another major benefit of using the Binance data is: nearly every part of our trading strategies can be completed within the same platform without delay in transferring the fund. So it reflects the real-time investment opportunities facing the traders.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also get the perpetual funding rate value from Binance. The funding rate is paid every 8 hours on Binance. So we have futures and spot prices every hour and realized funding rate payment at 8:00, 16:00, and 0:00 GMT each day. The perpetual and spot tradings are happening 24 hours per day and 7 days a week so there are no after-market hours in this market.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We get the earliest possible data on perpetual futures trading from Binance. The table below lists the starting and ending dates of our data for each crypto. Our data ends on 2022-11-13, covering the latest fallout of the FTX.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

<td id="S4.T2.2.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">2022-11-13</td>

</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Sample descriptions</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This table presents the sample start and end dates for the 5 cryptocurrencies and their total number of observations.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We obtain the trading costs from Binance’s website<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a> provides data on trading fees in perpetual futures and the spot market</span></span></span>. In general, the trading costs for the spot market are significantly larger than that for the perpetual futures for similar trading volume because futures typically are traded with leverage. Fee tiers are attributed to the 30-day trading volume. We attribute high trading costs with a 30-day spot trading volume above $1 million and futures trading volume above $15 million (small individual trader). Medium trading costs attribute to a 30-day spot trading volume above $150 million and futures trading volume above $1 billion (small funds). Low trading costs attribute to a 30-day spot trading volume above $2 billion and futures trading volume above 12.5 billion (large funds). No fee can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example for market makers. We consider trading costs for makers instead of takers because institutions typically trade maker orders.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
            Takers trade market orders while makers trade limit orders. Takers take liquidity from the market while makers make the market or provide liquidity to the market.</span></span></span> Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the specification of different trading costs. It also shows the random-maturity arbitrage bound for the deviation between the perpetual futures and the no-arbitrage price (<math id="S4.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>). The bounds become wider as the trading costs increase. Detailed explanations of the trading costs specifications are also provided in appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and Figure <a href="#Sx1.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To measure the deviation from the no-arbitrage price, we also obtain the interest rate data from Aave, a leading open-source DeFi liquidity protocol. Customers on Aave can either be a supplier or a borrower of cryptocurrencies. Because of the anonymity and decentralization of DeFi system, all borrowings are over-collateralized and the collateral can serve as an additional supply to the system for borrowing. The customers can also supply spare currencies to the system to earn an interest rate. The supply interest rate is typically different from the borrowing interest rate. Both interest rates and their wedge are determined algorithmically based on the market condition of supply and demand. We use interest rates from this platform because we believe it is a good proxy for the funding condition in the crypto market. Our results are robust if we use the interest rate from the traditional financial market.<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
            We also run our analysis using daily T-bill rates obtained from Kenneth French’s website at <a href="https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/Data_Library/f-f_factors.html</a>. The results are very close to ones using crypto market supply and borrowing rates.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our theory indicates using a risk-free rate available to the arbitrageurs. Therefore, we consider the interest rates on the stablecoins, which are not subject to volatile spot price movement and are the currency of denomination for perpetual futures margins. There are three major stablecoins traded on Aave: USDT, USDC, and DAI. To get a robust measure of the risk-free rate, we take an average of the three interest rates to arrive at our final risk-free supply and borrowing rate for the arbitrageurs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We plot the time-series evolvement of the interest rate in the appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. During the early years, we see higher interest rate volatility due to the funding liquidity of the DeFi platform. In later samples, interest rates are more stable and approach interest rates in traditional financial markets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Our interest rate data starts from 2020-01-08. Therefore, for coins with perpetual data available before the time (BTC and ETH), we begin the analysis from 2020-01-08. For other coins (BNB, DOGE, ADA), we begin the analysis from the time when they have data available.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="S4.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Trading costs specifications</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">The different trading costs tiers: no, low, medium, and high. Fee tiers are assigned based on past 30-day trading volume. High fees correspond to a 30-day trading volume above $1mn in spot and above $15mn in perpetuals, typically an individual trader. Medium fees attribute to a 30-day trading volume above $150mn in spot and above $1bn in perpetuals (small funds). Low fees attribute to a 30-day trading volume above $2bn in spot and above $12.5bn in perpetuals (large funds). The no fees tier can be negotiated with customized contracts, for example for market makers. We also report the theory implied no arbitrage bound (<math id="S4.T3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) for <math id="S4.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> under different trading costs specifications. They are calculated using the following formulas: <math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}=\kappa log\left(1-C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}=\kappa log\left(1-C\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}=\kappa log\left(1+C\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}=\kappa log\left(1+C\right)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.T3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is the round-trip percentage trading costs of the long-short strategy of perpetual and spot.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">To explain the deviation between perpetual futures and the spot, we also get the data of fear and greed index from alternative.me.<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://alternative.me/crypto/fear-and-greed-index/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://alternative.me/crypto/fear-and-greed-index/</a> provides the data on the fear and greed index</span></span></span> This index ranges from 0 to 100 and is constructed using past market return momentum, volatility, social media sentiment, the concentration of crypto market share, and google trends.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The focus of our empirical analysis is the annualized deviation <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as the interest rate that rationalizes an observed future-spot spread:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F=S\left(1+\frac{r+\rho}{\kappa}\right)\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mi>κ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F=S\left(1+\frac{r+\rho}{\kappa}\right)\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Using <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> to denote <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="log(F)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">log(F)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="log(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">log(S)</annotation></semantics></math> respectively, we obtain the following approximate equation for <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\approx\kappa(f-s)-r\ ." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\approx\kappa(f-s)-r\ .</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">This definition is the same in spirit to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al. (2018)</a></cite> who define the CIP deviation as the wedge that would equate the dollar borrowing rate and the synthetic dollar borrowing rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At each hour, we calculate <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> using data on the perpetual futures price, spot price, and the crypto risk-free interest rate. When the perpetual futures price is above the spot, an arbitrageur would short the futures and long the spot, and would finance her position by borrowing in the cash market (as is shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Therefore, we use the borrowing rate from Aave as the risk-free rate. On the other hand, when the perpetual futures price is below the spot, an arbitrageur would long the futures, short the spot, and invest the proceeds from shorting in the cash market (as is shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ 3 Arbitrage in Perpetual Futures ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). In such cases, we use the supply rate from Aave as the risk-free rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="S4.F3.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_figure_panel">
          
<div id="S4.F3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v3/fig1.svg" id="S4.F3.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/234;" width="476" height="234"></object>
</div>
        
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the 7-day moving averages of the annualized deviation of the perpetual futures-spot spread from the no-arbitrage benchmark for the five cryptocurrencies. The deviation <math id="S4.F3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as <math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v3/fig3.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/280;" width="476" height="280" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Correlation of <math id="S4.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, funding rate, spot returns and fear &amp; greed index</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F4.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the correlation among different crypto’s futures-spot deviation <math id="S4.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> (rows 1 to 5), funding rate (rows 6 to 10), fear &amp; greed index (row 11) and the spot returns (rows 12 to 16).</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the 7-day moving average of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> for each of the five cryptocurrencies. There is significant comovement in futures-spot spreads across all five cryptocurrencies, suggesting there exists a common factor driving the wedge. Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> confirms this finding: the futures-spot deviations are highly correlated across cryptocurrencies. This phenomenon highlights the integration of the cryptocurrency markets. One hypothesis is that the comovement in <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across various cryptocurrencies reflects time-varying funding constraints experienced by arbitrageurs in the market, as illustrated in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garleanu and Pedersen (2011)</a></cite>. Since arbitrageurs are marginal traders in all markets, their funding constraints are manifested in the <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across all cryptocurrency markets. Our theoretical and empirical analyses emphasize the importance of examining the object of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math>, as it sheds light on market stress and offers an estimate of the shadow costs associated with arbitrageurs’ trading and funding constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, from the demand side, the commonality in sentiment across different cryptocurrencies can also contribute to explaining the comovement of <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across different markets. From our theoretical analysis, arbitrageurs will only accommodate the demand in the market if the price deviation exceeds the trading and funding costs. Consequently, the overall sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot market manifests in the price gap between futures and spot. If the sentiment in different markets is driven by a common factor, we expect to observe a high comovement in the futures-spot spread. In Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we provide further analysis to explain the futures-spot spread. Our findings reveal that past returns of each cryptocurrency serve as significant explanatory variables for the time-series variation in the spread.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Interestingly, the correlation between deviations <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> and spot market returns is low. Although spot market returns are highly correlated among themselves, in line with the strong market factor results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite>, and no-arbitrage price deviations are highly correlated among themselves, it appears that different forces drive these distinct phenomena.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, we find that after the year 2022, futures-spot spreads become smaller in magnitude and less volatile compared to earlier years. The 7-day moving average stays around -50% most of the time for the 5 cryptocurrencies while larger sways in earlier years are quite common. This suggests the market is becoming increasingly efficient. In terms of the level of the deviation, which appears to stabilize in negative region, there can be two forces: (1) on the futures customer end, the relative end demand in the futures market is weaker compared to the spot; (2) for arbitrageurs, because of the lack of infrastructure to short the cryptos in the spot market (high shorting costs), their funding constraints would be larger in the negative region. All these forces contribute to the stabilization of the futures spot deviation around <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-50</annotation></semantics></math> percent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Last but not least, by design, <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is also highly correlated with the funding rate. The funding rate does not correlate perfectly with <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> because in real-world implementations: (1) there is a clamp region, within which the funding rate equals 0.01%; (2) the funding rate is calculated as a weighted average of futures-spot price deviations, with larger weight given to more recent observations; (3) in calculating the funding rate, Binance does not just consider the quote price, they also use an impact margin notional to consider price impact of the trade.<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
              
              
              
            See <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/support/faq/360033525031</a> for details of the funding rate calculation.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we provide a trading strategy motivated by our random-maturity arbitrage theory. Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports for different trading cost tiers, the bounds (<math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ρ</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) beyond which there exist random-maturity arbitrage opportunities. We consider a simple trading strategy: whenever <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> enters the region outside the annualized round-trip trading costs in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we open the position. We close the position when <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> first goes back to 0.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v3/figure_trading_theory_BTC.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/239;" width="476" height="239" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy: Bitcoin, high trading costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.F5.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.F5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Futures-spot deviations and trading thresholds of the random-maturity arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC under high trading costs. Each blue dot in the figure represents the annualized deviation of futures from the spot <math id="S4.F5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>. The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides an illustration of the trading strategy. When the deviation is beyond the orange lines, the strategy opens a trading position. The position is closed when the futures/spot deviation first hits the red line. We present trading thresholds across different trading costs for different currencies in Figure <a href="#Sx1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> in the appendix. Different trading strategies have the same close-position line which is equal to the risk-free rate while the open-position line adjusts to the level of trading costs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Since our trading strategy is a threshold trading rule, to annualize Sharpe ratios we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lucca and Moench (2015)</a></cite>, which considers a trading strategy that is only active on FOMC announcement dates. We first calculate the mean (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>) and standard deviation (<math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>) of our trading strategy during the time it is active. Next, we scale <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu/\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu/\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> by the number of periods the strategy is active in a year:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}\ ," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>μ</mi><mi>σ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.500em">,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">SR=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt{N_{a}}\ ,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> are average hourly returns and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> is the average number of hours the strategy is active in a year. We follow the same approach to annualize the returns and standard deviations: <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{ann}=\mu N_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{ann}=\mu N_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{ann}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{ann}=\sigma\sqrt{N_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<table id="S4.T4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T4.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"></th>

<tr id="S4.T4.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row"></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row"></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">No</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Low</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Medium</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">High</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T4.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">BTC</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">SR</span></th>
<td id="S4.T4.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3.94</span></td>

</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Performance of Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Performance under different trading cost tiers. The fees for spot (futures) are 2.25 (0.18) bps, 4.5 (0.72) bps, and 6.75 (1.44) bps for the low, medium, and high trading cost levels. Statistics reported are the annualized Sharpe ratio, return (%), volatility (%), max drawdown (%), alpha (%), t-stat of the alpha, proportion of time the strategy is active (%), and average open-to-close (OtC) position duration in hours.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents the strategy’s performance under different fee tiers. As trading costs decrease, the random-maturity arbitrage strategy engages in more active trading, leading to an increase in the SRs and a decrease in the average duration of open-to-close positions. The strategy also delivers highly significant alphas relative to the 3-factor model by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2022)</a></cite> and the 5-factor model by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cong et al. (2022a)</a></cite>. Evidently, the strategy’s performance cannot be explained by previously suggested risk factors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> zooms in and presents the trading performance of the strategy under high trading costs. We consider two cases: (1) unrestricted; (2) long-spot only. We consider the second case because, in earlier years of crypto derivatives, the infrastructure of shorting cryptocurrencies is not well-developed. We find that, as is implied by our theory, whenever the deviation between futures and spot is larger than the trading costs, performing a random-maturity arbitrage strategy would generate returns with high SR. After trading costs, the strategy generates a SR of 1.92 for BTC and much higher SRs for other cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Performance Over Time: High Trading Costs Tier</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the Sharpe ratios, annualized returns (%), standard deviations (%), and active percentages (%) of the random-maturity arbitrage trading strategies for five different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. We break down returns for each year and provide summary statistics across all time. The left panel shows the performance of the unrestricted trading strategy, where both long and short spot positions are allowed. The right panel shows the performance of the long-spot-only trading strategy, where shorting the spot is not allowed.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> also shows that as time goes by, the perpetual futures market seems to become more and more efficient. As we can see in 2022, the deviation of crypto price from the arbitrage-free bound is much less frequent compared to earlier years. But when the deviation happens, the resulting SR from the trade remains high.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing the results with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>, we find that deviations in crypto perpetual futures are considerably larger in magnitude. As a result, gains from the arbitrage strategies we study are also larger. Even though the volatility of the trading strategy also scales up, the Sharpe ratios in the crypto space are still larger than those in the traditional foreign exchange market as reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du, Tepper, and Verdelhan (2018)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">When a futures-spot gap opens up, gains from the trading strategy could potentially arise from two main sources: price convergence and funding rate payments. While industry publications usually emphasize the funding rate channel, we note that price convergence can generate quicker gains from arbitrage if dislocations are short-lived.
To examine these two sources empirically, in Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> we provide a decomposition of the trading strategy’s performance into price convergence versus funding rate payment. We find that price convergence plays a dominant role in total trading returns, while funding rate payments have a more minor role, which seems to diminish over time.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Return Decomposition: Price Convergence vs Funding Rate Payment for Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategies</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S4.T6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table decomposes the portfolio return into the part due to price convergence and the part due to funding rate payment.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The success of the trading strategy supports the theory of random-maturity arbitrage. Whenever there is a deviation larger than the gap implied by the theory, betting on convergence tends to generate a positive payoff at some uncertain future time. Therefore, the convergence arbitrage trade generates high Sharpe ratios.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Explaining Futures-spot Deviations</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Deviations of perpetual futures from no-arbitrage benchmarks ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we observe a strong common comovement of the futures-spot deviation across all crypto assets. Our goal is to understand the fundamental forces driving this common factor. We consider two potential hypotheses: (1) the time-varying funding constraints of arbitrageurs, and (2) the time-varying relative demand from end-users for perpetual futures compared to the spot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both forces could potentially explain these patterns. Arbitrageurs will accommodate the relative demand from end-users only until the price deviation lies within the random-maturity no-arbitrage bound, which depends on arbitrageurs’ funding conditions. As arbitrageurs are likely the marginal investors in all cryptocurrency markets, their time-varying funding constraints may create common time-series variation in <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> across different cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, when the deviation lies within the no-arbitrage bound, variations in demand from the perpetual futures market compared to the spot market will influence the price deviation. It is plausible that relative demand has common factors across different cryptocurrencies. For instance, sentiment could drive their common variation, as perpetual futures allow for high leverage, which attracts overconfident, extrapolative, and sentiment-driven investors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Determining which of the two factors better explains the observed price deviation is an empirical question. To shed light on this, we use past returns as a proxy for relative extrapolative demand in the perpetual futures market compared to the spot market. Past returns correlate with the demand from investors with extrapolative beliefs, who are more likely to trade in the perpetual futures market given the high leverage it provides. Therefore, past returns would correlate with the relative demand in the perpetual futures market compared to the spot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For the time-varying funding constraint, we consider using crypto return volatility as a proxy, because, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Adrian and Shin (2010)</a></cite>, arbitrageurs likely face Value-at-Risk (VaR) type constraints, which are more likely to bind when market volatility is high.</p>
</div>

<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Regression of the futures-spot gap against explanatory variables</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S5.T7.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="S5.T7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We present regression results of <math id="S5.T7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on the past four months’ annualized returns (Ret) and volatility (Vol) for Bitcoin and Ethereum. The left panel reports results for Bitcoin, and the right panel reports results for Ethereum. For each cryptocurrency, we consider three models: (1) regressing <math id="S5.T7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns; (2) regressing <math id="S5.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on past volatility; and (3) regressing <math id="S5.T7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on both past returns and volatility. The observations are at a daily frequency. The sample period spans from January 30, 2020, to November 13, 2022, totaling 1,011 days.
