We report HAC-robust t-statistics in parentheses. <math id="S5.T7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="*p&lt;.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">*p&lt;.1</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T7.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="**p&lt;.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">**p&lt;.05</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.T7.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="***p&lt;.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∗</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">***p&lt;.01</annotation></semantics></math></span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 5 Explaining Futures-spot Deviations ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> presents the regression results of <math id="S5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> on past returns, volatility, and both for BTC and ETH. The regression coefficients on past returns are positive and highly significant. This suggests that when past returns are high, perpetual futures exhibit a more positive deviation against the spot. Mapping this back to our second hypothesis, when past returns are high, the demand for futures relative to the spot is also likely to be high. Consequently, even after arbitrageurs accommodate the demand outside of trading costs, the residual demand still manifests itself through the perpetual-spot deviation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu and Tsyvinski (2021)</a></cite> document a significant time-series momentum pattern in the crypto market. Given that positive past returns lead to a positive gap between futures and spot prices, it is worth examining further whether the time-series momentum phenomenon is driven by margin trading and price pressure from the perpetual futures market. We leave this as an open question for future research.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We find that volatility does not significantly covary with the futures and spot deviation. This suggests that it is not the time-varying funding constraints of arbitrageurs that drive the comovement in futures-spot deviations across different cryptocurrencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, a prerequisite for the gap between futures and spot prices to occur is the existence of trading costs for arbitrageurs. Arbitrage trading will accommodate all the demand in the futures until the price deviation lies within a trading cost bound. Within the bound, the relative demand of futures compared to the spot will still manifest itself in the deviation of futures prices from the spot. Due to the comovement of the time-varying relative demand, we observe a significant common factor in crypto future-spot deviations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Perpetual futures play an important role in today’s crypto markets and could potentially be adopted in non-crypto markets in the future. Understanding the fundamental mechanism of this financial derivative is a crucial first step for understanding speculation and hedging dynamics in this fast-evolving area. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the arbitrage and funding rate payment mechanisms that underpin perpetual futures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In an ideal, frictionless world, we show that arbitrageurs would trade perpetual futures in such a way that a constant relationship exists between the future price and the spot price. In the presence of trading costs, the deviation of the futures price to the spot would lie within a bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the theory, we then empirically examine the comovement of the futures-spot spread across different cryptocurrencies and implement a theory-motivated arbitrage strategy. We find that this simple strategy yields substantial Sharpe ratios across various trading cost scenarios. The evidence supports our theoretical argument that perpetual futures-spot spreads exceeding trading costs represent a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we provide an explanation for the common comovement in futures-spot spreads across different crypto-currencies: arbitrageurs can only accommodate market demand if the price deviation exceeds trading costs. As a result, the overall sentiment in the futures market relative to the spot market is reflected in the spread.
Our empirical findings suggest that past return momentum can account for a significant portion of the time-series variation in the futures-spot spread.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Trading costs tiers for the spot market</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F7.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the trading costs tiers for the crypto spot market from Binance: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a>. Our high, medium, and low trading cost specification corresponds to VIP 1, VIP 5, and VIP 8 tiers as illustrated with red rectangles in the picture. The 30-day trading volume requirements for VIP 1, 5, and 8 are 1 million, 150 million, and 2 billion respectively in the spot market. We consider the trading costs for makers as institutions typically trade maker orders. Binance offers a temporary discount for VIP 4-8 to have the same trading cost as VIP 9. We consider the non-discounted trading costs to make the comparison more reliable and fair.</span></p></div></div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Trading costs tiers for the perp market</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F8.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx1.F8.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents the trading costs tiers for the crypto perpetual market from Binance: <a href="https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.binance.com/en/fee/trading</a>. Our high, medium, and low trading cost specification corresponds to VIP 1, VIP 5, and VIP 8 tiers as illustrated with red rectangles in the picture. The 30-day trading volume requirements for VIP 1, 5, and 8 are 15 million, 1 billion, and 12.5 billion respectively in the perpetual market. We consider the trading costs for makers as institutions typically trade maker orders.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F9" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v3/figures/exchanges_fr_ethereum.png" id="Sx1.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/186;" width="476" height="186" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Ether annualized funding rate across exchanges</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F9.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">The figure presents the 7-day moving average annualized funding rate for Ether (ETH) across exchanges. The data is obtained from glassnode, an analytics platform. The data covers two major market turbulences: the COVID stock market crash from February to April 2020, and the FTX insolvency in November 2022. The FTX collapse led to significant negative funding rates on all solvent exchanges, thus the perpetual future prices were lower than the spot prices on the solvent exchanges. Vice versa on the insolvent FTX. The funding rates become more volatile after the event, indicating increased uncertainty for the market participants.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="Sx1.F10" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Annualized interest rate from Aave</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx1.F10.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure presents the daily supply and borrowing rate from Aave. We consider three stablecoins: USDT, USDC, and DAI. Each day, we take the average interest rate of the 3 crypto stablecoins to get the proxy for the risk-free funding rate of the arbitrageurs. The averaging removes the idiosyncratic noise in borrowing and supply in individual stablecoins. The sample period is from 2020-01-08 to 2022-11-13.</p></div></div>
</figure>

<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the main text of our paper, we demonstrate the profitability of a simple theory-motivated trading strategy. The trading threshold can also be potentially further improved using a data-driven approach. In this part, we implement a data-driven two-threshold arbitrage trading strategy in the perpetual futures market. The strategy can be characterized with a tuple of two thresholds: <math id="Sx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="Sx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the upper bar and <math id="Sx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the lower bar, <math id="Sx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u&gt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u&gt;l</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="Sx2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&gt;u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&gt;u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the spot and short the futures. When <math id="Sx2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-l&lt;\rho&lt;l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-l&lt;\rho&lt;l</annotation></semantics></math>, we close the position. When <math id="Sx2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&lt;-u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&lt;-u</annotation></semantics></math>, we long the futures and short the spot. Figure <a href="#Sx2.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> presents an illustration of the strategy for Bitcoin with the trading thresholds estimated using real-time data.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx2.F16" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2212.06888v3/figure_trading_4_btc.png" id="Sx2.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/239;" width="476" height="239" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 16: </span>Two-threshold trading strategy: Bitcoin, high trading costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx2.F16.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx2.F16.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This figure presents real-time trading thresholds of the arbitrage strategy we implement for BTC under high trading costs. Each blue dot in the figure represents annualized deviation of futures from the spot <math id="Sx2.F16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho=\kappa(f-s)-r</annotation></semantics></math>. The orange line is the open-position threshold and the red line is the close-position threshold.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To determine the optimal <math id="Sx2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(u,l)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(u,l)</annotation></semantics></math>, at the beginning of each month, we calculate the returns of the two-threshold trading strategy based on the past 6 months’ data on a grid of parameters. From Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we find the theory implied bounds for price deviation across all trading costs specifications lie within <math id="Sx2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-200\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Sx2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+200\%</annotation></semantics></math>. So we choose the grid as increasing from <math id="Sx2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="Sx2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200\%</annotation></semantics></math> with an incremental step of <math id="Sx2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="Sx2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Sx2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="Sx2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u\geq l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u\geq l</annotation></semantics></math>). In total, there are <math id="Sx2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="210" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>210</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">210</annotation></semantics></math> model specifications. We choose the model that delivers the highest Sharpe Ratio in the validation sample of the past 6 months.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx2.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> presents the real-time trading thresholds of our arbitrage strategy for BTC under high trading costs. To mitigate the trading cost, the strategy automatically chooses a much lower close-position threshold compared to the open-position threshold. We also present the visualization of all trading strategies under different trading costs in appendix Figure <a href="#Sx1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> to <a href="#Sx1.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>. Under no-trading costs, the strategy chooses a low open-position threshold and the open- and close-position thresholds coincide with each other. Since there is no trading cost, the strategy no longer needs to wait for price convergence to avoid high turnover. On the contrary, with high trading costs, the strategy chooses a larger open-position threshold and a smaller close-position threshold. This reflects the automatic adjustment from the algorithm for trading costs and turnovers.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#Sx2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> presents the return statistics for this strategy under high trading costs over time. In the baseline ‘unrestricted’ strategy, we allow for both (1) longing the futures and shorting the spot and (2) shorting the futures and longing the spot while in the ‘long-spot only’ strategy, we only allow for shorting the futures and longing the spot. The reason we consider the ‘long-spot only’ strategy is the infrastructure for shorting the spot is not well-developed. So we want to examine the performance of the trading strategy in the presence of such limits to arbitrage.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx2.T8" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Portfolio Performance: High Trading Cost</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx2.T8.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx2.T8.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the annual return, standard deviations, Sharpe ratios of the two-threshold trading strategies for the 5 different cryptocurrencies with high trading costs. We also report the proportion of time the trading strategy has an open position. We break down returns into each year and also provide summary stat across all time. The left panel shows the performance of the unrestricted trading strategy where both long and short spot is allowed. The right panel shows the performance of the long-spot-only trading strategy where shorting the spot is not allowed.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We find the arbitrage trading strategy has a high Sharpe ratio under high trading costs. The annualized Sharpe ratio for Bitcoin is 1.78 in our sample. They are even higher for other cryptos. The high Sharpe ratio of the trading strategy corroborates our theoretical results that when the price deviation is large enough, the trading would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In the year 2022, the deviation between the futures and the spot becomes smaller and less volatile. There seems to be a structural break. We indeed find the trading strategy takes less active positions and significantly lower annualized returns. However, when there is a large enough deviation, the strategy can still generate sizeable Sharpe ratios in trading.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The conclusion and results remain similar if we consider ‘long-spot only’ trading strategies where only shorting the futures and longing the spot is allowed. Considering this one-sided trade slightly lowers the Sharpe ratio but the algorithm automatically adjusts by increasing the proportion of times being active. The resulting annualized returns increase. In the year 2022, since most of the time, the futures price is below the spot and we don’t allow longing the futures and shorting the spot trade, the proportion of time the strategy is active is very low.</p>
</div>

<td id="Sx2.T9.2.21.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right">3.77</td></tr>
<tr id="Sx2.T9.2.22" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="Sx2.T9.2.22.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"></th>
<th id="Sx2.T9.2.22.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb">SR</th>
<td id="Sx2.T9.2.22.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">16.47</td>
<td id="Sx2.T9.2.22.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">8.90</td>
<td id="Sx2.T9.2.22.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">5.07</td>
<td id="Sx2.T9.2.22.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">3.04</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Portfolio Performance under Different Trading Costs</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx2.T9.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx2.T9.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table presents the portfolio performance under different trading cost specifications. The fee for spot is 0, 1.5 bps, 3.75 bps, and 5.25 bps for the 4 trading costs specifications. The fee for the futures are 0, 0, 0.54 bp, 1.08 bps for the 4 trading costs specifications.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#Sx2.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> further reports the performance of the trading strategy under different trading costs specifications laid out in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Data ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. The results from Table <a href="#Sx2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> correspond to the last column in Table <a href="#Sx2.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>. As trading costs increase, our trading strategy dynamically adjusts by lowering the proportion of time being active. The annualized return decreases and annualized standard deviation are of similar magnitude across different trading costs. As a result, SR decreases as trading costs increase. Under no trading cost, we see a Sharpe ratio of 6.72 for BTC and Sharpe ratios above 10 for all other cryptos. This also confirms our theoretical results that when there is no trading cost, any deviation of perpetual price from the no-arbitrage benchmark would be a random-maturity arbitrage opportunity.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing Table <a href="#Sx2.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> with Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Random-maturity Arbitrage Strategy ‣ 4 Data and Empirical Analysis ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we find under low and no trading costs, the potential incremental benefits from using a data-driven two-threshold trading rule are much larger compared to higher trading costs. The intuition can be easily illustrated by comparing the empirical real-time trading thresholds in the theory-motivated strategy and the data-driven strategy under low trading costs (Figure <a href="#Sx1.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> and Figure <a href="#Sx1.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ A. Additional figures and tables ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>). With persistent <math id="Sx2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> the data-driven approach can find the optimal close-position threshold corresponding to the level of <math id="Sx2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> while the theory-motivated one is too conservative in setting a close-position threshold equal to 0.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">There are two sources of trading profit for our trading strategy: (1) the price convergence; (2) the funding rate payment. In Table <a href="#Sx2.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ B. Data-driven Arbitrage Strategy ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, we decompose the return to our trading strategy without trading cost into the two sources. We find across different cryptos, the return from price convergence accounts for a larger proportion of the total profit. For BTC, the price convergence accounts for more than <math id="Sx2.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2/3</annotation></semantics></math> of the profits, and for ETH, it accounts for about <math id="Sx2.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3/4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3/4</annotation></semantics></math>. Additionally, the decomposition for the year 2022 generates different patterns, the return due to funding rate plays a much smaller role across different cryptos. This is because the deviation from perpetual to spot is much smaller during the year. The results suggest when more sophisticated arbitrageurs enter the market, the large deviation of perpetual from the spot would be more of an off-equilibrium outcome. As a result, the funding rate payment will also be small.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 10: </span>Return Decomposition: Price Convergence vs Funding Rate Payment</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx2.T10.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel"><span id="Sx2.T10.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This table decomposes the portfolio return into the part due to price convergence and the part due to funding rate payment.</span></p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="Sx2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">In all, our analysis of the trading strategy demonstrates the profitability of perpetual-spot arbitrage trade. The deviation of the futures to spot can also serve as an important measure for the frictions, trading costs, and limits to arbitrage in the market.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">C. High-frequency event study of funding rate payment</h2>

<div id="Sx3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this part, we provide a high-frequency event study around the funding rate payment time. We hope to further understand the microstructure effect of the funding rate mechanism on perpetual futures pricing. We obtain 1-min BTC, ETH, and DOGE price data from Kaiko. We then calculate the return from a strategy that taps into the funding rate payment with a window of -4 hours and +4 hours around the funding rate payment. When the funding rate is positive, we stay on the short side of the perpetual futures to receive the funding rate and long the spot to hedge the risk. When the funding rate is negative, we do the trade in the opposite direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#Sx3.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ C. High-frequency event study of funding rate payment ‣ Fundamentals of Perpetual Futures" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> presents the average ex-funding-rate cumulative returns of such a strategy around the time of funding rate payment for BTC, ETH, and DOGE. We see when the funding rate is positive, there is a significant price drop. This reflects the efficiency of the market. When traders observe almost certain positive funding rate payments. They have incentives to short the futures and long the spot. This behavior results in a large decline in spot-perpetual return, which offsets the profits from gaining the funding rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On the other hand, we observe less-significant price drops around negative funding rate payments. This can be due to 2 reasons: (1) in our sample, only around 15% of the sample has a negative funding rate and the magnitude is smaller than the positive funding rate. A small sample would result in noisy estimates making it more difficult to discover the patterns in the positive case. (2) To implement the arbitrage strategy, the traders need to long the futures and short the spot. However, the infrastructure for shorting the spot is not well-developed for the crypto spot market. Trading in the futures market alone would expose the traders to too much risk. Because of these limits to arbitrage, we observe a more muted price decline around negative funding rate payments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Even if the price shows a large decline at high-frequency, it is worth inspecting how much trading profit is left from exploiting the funding rate payment. We implement a high-frequency funding rate arbitrage strategy. Five minutes before the funding rate payment, we are going to open the position in the futures and spot market. We close the position 5 minutes after the funding rate payment.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We found that the average one-time return from implementing the strategy is about 1.5 bps, which sums up to 16.4% per year. However, implementing the strategy requires round-trip trading in the spot market which has a total trading cost of 3 bps even under low trading cost specification. Therefore after accounting for trading costs, the trading profits will be attenuated. The price movement in perpetual and spot attenuates about <math id="Sx3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{3}</annotation></semantics></math> of the original profits from receiving the funding rate across the three different cryptos.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Sx3.F17" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2212.06888v3/funding_rate_event_study-eps-converted-to.svg" id="Sx3.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/409;" width="476" height="409"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 17: </span>High-frequency Event Study around the Funding Rate Payment time for BTC, ETH, and DOGE</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="Sx3.F17.2" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel">This figure shows cumulative returns to strategies that try to exploit the funding rate payment at the 1-minute frequency for BTC, ETH, and DOGE. The strategies returns reported in the figure do not include the funding rate payment, similar to the ex-dividend returns to stock around the dividend payment. The blue line shows cumulative return to a strategy that shorts the futures and longs the spot when the funding rate is positive. The orange line shows cumulative return to a strategy that longs the futures and shorts the spot when the funding rate is negative.</p></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</article>
</div>
</div>
